div.p: Testing for a structural break in the weight matrix of the spatial error or spatial lag model. Spatial Economic Analysis. This paper studies the weight matrix in the two generic spatial econometric models, allowing the friction-of-distance parameter to be freely estimated by (Gaussian) maximum likelihood. It shows that in samples of moderate size it is perfectly feasible to estimate both the distance-decay coefficient that shapes the weights, and the usual SEM/SLM coefficient, and to test for a change in the former at an unknown change point. The procedure is easily extended to test for changes in other parameters. Tests of empirical size and power are investigated by Monte Carlo experiment, and the test is applied to a model of exchange rate pass through, with clear results.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: This paper introduces a test for a change over time in the structure of spatial interaction in the cross-section dimension of panel data. The setting is a fully parametric regression model, either the spatial error model (SEM) or the spatial lag model (SLM), where the interaction matrix is of known functional form but depends on a parameter that is to be estimated from one or more cross-sections of a panel. We examine the performance of tests in which the maintained hypothesis is parameter constancy over time, and the alternative is a change to the parameter(s) (a structural break) at a single unknown point in time. We focus attention on the parameter that determines the shape of the spatial interaction matrix in our set-up, though the approach we adopt is quite general, and can easily be adapted to test for changes to other parameters that may be of interest, as we illustrate in the empirical application. We do not assume that any parameters are known to the researcher, but in practice there may be quite strong prior grounds for suspecting that a structural break has occurred in a certain period. Such breaks might, for example, be triggered by domestic political events, like changes in the degree of local control over taxation, or a regional independence referendum, or economic development such as the upgrading of public transport links, or broader international movements reflected in the erection or removal of trade barriers, or anticipated changes in distance frictions more generally (on this latter possibility, see Brun, Carrère, Guillaumont, & de Melo, 2005, and the surrounding debate). This paper uses the SEM and SLM models to illustrate our method because they are often used, and because if our approach is to be feasible more widely, it must be seen to work in these cases. The essence of the approach is to compare the maximized value of the model's likelihood when no break is allowed with the value that is attained when the parameter (or parameters) of interest is (are) allowed to change, taking possibly different values after some date. The approach works by estimating all the relevant parameters by maximum likelihood (ML), and computing a likelihood ratio at every point in some search interval of potential break dates. The approximate sampling distribution of the resulting ML ratio has been worked out by Andrews (1993), and can be used to construct a formal test for the existence of a break. The present paper first investigates the properties of this test, principally its power and significance level when the sampling distributions tabulated by Andrews (2003) are used. Then our procedure is applied to the case of the exchange rate pass-through (ERPT) hypothesis for a collection of 10 countries in the euro area. The reason for suspecting a break may have occurred in that case is the introduction of the common currency.

It is usual in the spatial econometric literature to treat the matrix W when present as fixed a priori. It is also widely accepted that this is unsatisfactory, and so researchers often report informal attempts to test the effects of this assumption, for example, by considering several different versions of W and comparing the results. This approach is exemplified by the work of Páez, Scott, and Volz (2008), and Le Gallo, Ertur, and Baumont (2003), among many. Some authors such as Stetzer (1982), Florax and Rey (1995), Griffith and Lagona (1998), and Stakhovych and Bijmolt (2009) consider misspecified W experimentally, while a more formal analysis is now possible by applying the non-nested testing method described by Kelejian and Piras (2011). Very much in the same spirit, Case, Rosen, and Hines (1993) consider weight matrices that are linear combinations of two given matrices, W = aW a + (1 -a)W b , and estimate a by maximum likelihood estimator (MLE). More recently, Bhattacharjee and Jensen-Butler (2013) and Ahrens and Bhattacharjee (2015) develop consistent algorithms to estimate an unknown W matrix from a panel dataset, whereas Lee and Yu (2012) consider estimation in the presence of an exogenously given sequence of weights matrices, and Kelejian and Piras (2014) and Qu and Lee (2015) make significant advances in the treatment of endogenous weighting matrices, also in a panel setting. So far as we are aware, however, there has as yet been no systematic investigation of the possibility of fully estimating W parametrically from the data for a single period, except for the work reported in Benjanuvatra and Burridge (2015). The present work demonstrates by numerical experiment that for W of the forms commonly adopted, not only is such estimation often feasible by MLE but also the small sample properties of a test for the constancy of such a W over time against the alternative of a single parametric break at an unknown date are highly satisfactory. 1 This paper's approach is model based, and treats 'distance' friction parametrically; this is a choice on our part, and it is certainly possible to study the structural change issue in a variety of other ways, including the decomposition of a data or residual covariance matrix advanced by Bhattacharjee and Jensen-Butler (2013), or a variety of procedures that compare one form of interaction matrix with another, as discussed by Angulo, Burridge, and Mur (2017). We would expect researchers to adopt whichever approach seems best suited to their chosen modelling environment, and we do not attempt to solve that implicit decision problem. Our purpose is rather to propose, illustrate and evaluate one particular approach that we believe has merit.

The foundations on which the present approach rests are in Andrews' (1993) development of the distribution theory for extremum-based tests for structural breaks at unknown change points, and in the application of the ML method to estimate the distance friction parameter in the SLM discussed in Benjanuvatra and Burridge (2015). In the next section we set up the models and describe the data structure assumed, together with technical assumptions sufficient to ensure identification and consistent estimation of the relevant parameters. The third section describes the structural break tests, while the features of the problem to be explored numerically, and some illustrative simulation results, are in the fourth section. Application to the case of ERPT for 10 European countries is described in the fifth section, which some readers might want to read first, and tentative conclusions are given in the sixth section. All computations have been done using algorithms written by the authors and run in MATLAB; these will be made available from our webpages. 2

div.head: Introduction
div.p: We suppose that a 'spatially' structured panel of data is available; in each time period there is thus a cross-section of observations, which are assumed to have been generated by either the SEM or SLM. We are not concerned here with choosing between these two model forms; rather they are both included to show that the approach can be applied to either. It is further supposed that while the same model form applies throughout the data record, there may be a change in the parameter values at some point in time. This paper presents an approach for the detection of such a change affecting the spatial interaction matrix, W, when there is uncertainty about the date at which the change occurs. There may be situations in which the ability to handle more than one change point would be desirable, and indeed researchers might have quite sophisticated priors about such potential change points, while smooth evolutionary changes might be more plausible in many settings.

The multiple unknown change-point problem might be considered as a possible avenue for future research using the approach due to Bai and Perron (1998), and smooth transitions could be studied along the lines surveyed by Tong (2011); seen in that context, this paper takes but a first step, albeit an essential one. As with all new statistical procedures, adoption of our proposals will depend on their utility in practice, and exploring this for the single-unknown-change-point case is our main focus.

Our tests are constructed by comparing the ML when the null hypothesis is imposed, that is, no break is allowed, with the ML allowing one or more of the parameters to change at some time point in the sample. The time at which the likelihood ratio is found to be greatest is the candidate break point, and the test compares this ML ratio with critical values from Andrews (2003). In finite samples, the relevant sampling distributions are unknown, and so an important practical question has to be addressed numerically. Before recommending adoption of the tests we must establish that the nominal significance level is reasonably accurate. Here, we focus on 5% but the qualitative results are similar at other levels. As will become apparent, the data structure we envisage is such that a great deal of numerical computation is required to evidence the reliability of our proposals; in reporting our experiments, encouraged by the editor and referees, we have sought to minimize the number of tables that are filled with estimates that 'should' be 5% or 100% when all is well in favour of summary descriptions.

div.head: Formal assumptions, asymptotics and estimator consistency
div.p: Technical conditions under which the parameters of the SEM and SLM described above can be consistently estimated from a single cross-section as the number of observation sites, n, increases, which extend Lee's (2004) results, can be found in Benjanuvatra and Burridge (2015). In broad terms, the need to estimate rather than impose a value for the distance friction parameter, g, leads to a requirement that a number of Lee's conditions hold for every g in a compact set that includes the true value. In Benjanuvatra and Burridge, asymptotics are discussed for the case, T = 1, n 1, that is, of a single cross-section with an increasing number of sites, and with W row-normalized; in the present panel setting, the more relevant case is where the time span increases while the cross-section dimension is fixed, that is, T 1, n constant, as this better reflects the data structure usually encountered. With the assumption of time independence of the cross-section disturbances, these two cases are more similar than might at first appear. To see this, consider the case in which the cross-section dimension increases in such a way that the weight matrix, now denoted W N , is block diagonal, composed of T identical non-interacting subsystems each with n sites, and weight matrices, W n , so that N = T × n, leading to:
Observe that the eigenvalues of W N are T copies of those of W n , that

div.head: Definitions of the tests
div.p: Except where otherwise indicated, from here on asymptotic will mean, 'as T 1 for given n'. The objective is to test for a break at an unknown date; if in fact the potential break date, t, were known, a simple likelihood ratio test would be feasible, of the form:
div.formula: LR (t) = 2 (L a (t) + L b (t) -L R (T )) (15
div.p: in which the quantities on the right-hand side are the maximized values of the log-likelihoods as defined above. In large samples, with (T , t) 1, and under the conditions described in section 2.3, this object has a chi-square null distribution with 1 degree of freedom (d.f.). However, in general we think it is more interesting to suppose that the date, t, is not known exactly. Building on Hawkins (1987), the ground-breaking paper of Andrews (1993) studies the behaviour of objects like Sup t {LR(t)}, the largest value the likelihood ratio takes over the chosen range of potential break dates, {t}. The Sup t {LR(t)} will have the large sample distribution tabulated by Andrews, provided that the likelihood ratio has the usual chi-squared asymptotic distribution, which in turn holds under the conditions given by Benjanuvatra and Burridge (2015), as modified above. The experiments reported in section 4 investigate numerically the empirical significance levels (designated as 'size' in the tables) and powers of the decision rules given by referring Sup t {LR(t)} to critical values from Andrews' distributions.

To anticipate slightly, we find the decision rules are generally conservative for small T , that is, have actual probabilities of type 1 error lower than their nominal significance levels, but nevertheless seem to have impressive power to detect a change in g.

Once it is accepted that a potential break date is unknown, it becomes natural to consider searching for a break in a sub-interval of [1, T ]. For convenience here, and to connect our finite sample tests to the correct asymptotic critical values, we map discrete t-intervals into intervals in (0, 1). Suppose we wish to test for a break in the interval, T 1 ≤ t ≤ T 2 ; setting p 1 = T 1 /T and p 2 = T 2 /T we represent this interval as p = [p 1 , p 2 ] [ (0, 1) where the latter interval remains bounded away from 0 and 1 (important in the asymptotics as explained by Andrews, 1993, p. 839). As T 1, the asymptotic distributions are approached as p is held fixed. As the width of the search interval increases, so the asymptotic null distribution of the Sup statistic moves to the right. Andrews also shows, however, that this distribution depends on p 1 and p 2 only through the quantity, l = p 2 (1-p 1 ) p 1 (1-p 2 ) ; this permits critical values calculated for symmetric intervals [p 1 , 1 -p 1 ] to be applied more widely using interpolation in l (see Andrews, 1993, pp. 839-840, for details). To implement a test we thus fix T , T 1 and T 2 , compute p 1 p 2 and the ratio, l, and refer to tables in Andrews (2003) to interpolate the required critical value. To represent the tests whose performance we simulate, therefore, we define the generic test statistic as:
div.formula: Sup p{LR(t)}.(16)

div.head: Design
div.p: Without the benefit of a fully developed sampling theory for the likelihood, or indeed for any of the parameter estimates, and in the absence of any pivotal statistics, it is evident that many factors could in principle affect the performance of the structural break tests. The performance aspects on which we have decided to concentrate are empirical size and power for the null hypothesis of 'no break' versus the alternative of 'a break somewhere'.

In an ideal world, under the null hypothesis, no matter whereabouts in the parameter space we look, the significance level of the test for a break would be equal to the nominal level chosen. Similarly, the power to detect departures from the null should ideally be high everywhere. Of course, neither will be true in practice: given that the reference distributions for the statistics are only valid for T large, there will be variations in empirical significance levels across the parameter space, and large breaks are more easily detected than small ones. The question to be resolved is therefore whether or not the tests will be reliable enough for use in empirical work, rather than whether or not they are optimal tests. Factors that could affect test performance are regional shape, design matrix, X, and n, T , t, T 1 , T 2 , r, g a , g b , f (d i,j ), and s 2 , width and location of the search interval, p, and finally whether parameters other than g might have changed during the study period. It could also be anticipated that results for the SLM and SEM might differ in some systematic way (happily, they do not, though the tests are slightly less conservative for the SLM in many cases).

The strategy we adopted was to investigate some of these dimensions for particular cases in preliminary experiments, and then to focus most of our effort on establishing how the tests might behave in samples of the size relevant for empirical exercises. Because the computational burden of the experiments is unusually heavy, the number of replications used in the various cases we report is fixed at 4800 (this is 300 on each of 16 parallel processor cores). The approximate standard error of the estimated empirical significance level is therefore: a(1 -a)/reps ≈ 0.003 (a = 5%), which is accurate enough for current purposes. The cases that we investigated for the SEM span the following dimensions:
• Time dimension: sample sizes T [ {11, 25, 100, 250}.
• Space dimension: sample sizes n [ {16, 49, 100, 400}.

• p-dimension: all breaks, when present, were placed in the centre of the record, but the test intervals varied in width and location as in Table 1, to reveal the effect of greater prior certainty about the location of any possible break. Thus, for example, with T = 25, there is either no break (the null hypothesis), or a break at T = 13. The researcher does not know the date exactly, and so has to search over an interval; the intervals we trialled for this case were [T 1 , T 2 ] = [5, 7], [7, 13], [5,21], [9, 17], and [12, 14]; that is, in the first interval the researcher is mistaken about the break date, in the second the date is at the upper end of the interval, and in the third, fourth and fifth intervals the researcher has progressively better prior knowledge. The pattern of results that emerged was as might be expected, and we report only results for p5 in any detail, some comments on the other intervals trialled being relegated to the Appendix in the supplemental data online.
• Variance of disturbance relative to the scale of the regressors s 2 [ {.025, .25, 4}this had little if any effect.

• Spatial parameter values (r, g) [ {0.0, + 0.2, + 0.4, + 0.6, + 0.8} × {1, 2, 3}; we are grateful to an editor and referees for encouraging us to examine negative correlation captured by r , 0 and a failure of identification of g when r = 0. In the latter case the issue is whether the test outcome is likely to be misleading; we find that generally it is not, because the tests continue to have approximately correct significance level. • Functional form of W. We tested both exponential and inverse power of distance weights; there was no systematic difference as we report below. We kept the exogenous regressor dimension fixed at k = 3, with x ti1 = 1, x ti2 and x ti3 drawn from N ( 0, I 2 ) for t = 1, . . . , T i = 1, . . . , n; and the regional shape adopted was one square interconnected region with side n 1/2 .

For T [ {25, 100, 250} there were five tests conducted at each of three nominal significance levels, a [ {0.10, 0.05, 0.01}. The critical values were calculated using Andrews (2003, tab. 1, p. 396) and interpolation in l as described in Andrews (1993). For the SLM, a smaller set of experiments was conducted, since it rapidly emerged that the tests were more powerful in this case than in the SEM, yet retained their generally conservative size (i.e., they had empirical significance levels no greater than the nominal levels in most cases).

Test performance across various dimensions Time As the number of time periods for which data are available increases, so we expect any structural break that may be present to be more easily detected. To explore this for a small spatial system we report simulations of the SEM with s 2 = 0.25, for n = 16, T = 11, 25, 100, 250, test interval p5 for two cases.

In each case, the null hypothesis to be tested is that there is no change in g, i.e., H 0 :g b = g a , but g is unknown and so must be estimated along with the other parameters, and also unknown is the potential break date, t = t. The alternatives reported in the table depart from the null in only one dimension, that is, H A :g b = g a where the change takes place at date, t = t. The point of the exercise is to reveal how the significance level and the power of the test are affected by the time span of data available. To illustrate this aspect it is thus convenient to use cases with strong to moderate positive spatial correlation, such as the following:
div.formula: Case 1: r a = r b = 0.6, g a = g b = 1; Alternative 1A: r a = r b = 0.6, g a = 1, g b = 2; Alternative 1B: r a = r b = 0.6, g a = 1, g b = 3 Case 2: r a = r b = 0.8, g a = g b = 1; Alternative 2A: r a = r b = 0.8, g a = 1, g b = 2; Alternative 2B: r a = r b = 0.8, g a = 1, g b = 3
div.p: The results are summarized in Table 2. The tests are quite conservative in all cases, as the empirical sizes are below 5%, but size improves towards its asymptotic value as T increases. Even though the search intervals were kept deliberately tighter for these cases, the low power for T = 11, 25 is expected as each cross-section, with n = 16, is very small. The larger r value in Case 2 roughly doubles the power for small T , while the larger break in alternatives 1B and 2B is clearly more easily detected. Note that here and in subsequent tables the p5 test assumes the user has a fairly accurate prior about the break location (to within 10% of the total time span for T = 25, 100 or 250). Attainable powers are lower when the search interval is wider.

div.head: Space
div.p: Larger cross-sections should produce sharper parameter estimates, making a break easier to detect for any given time span of data. To illustrate this, we report results for test interval p5 for the same cases as in Table 2, but now with T = 25, and n = 16, 49, 100, 400.

Here, T = 25, a moderate value, while all the n trialled might be considered 'small' space dimensions. For n ≥ 49 the test powers are strikingly good, though notably higher when r is higher, as in Case 2. These results indicate that when there is medium or strong positive spatial correlation, with a time span of 25 or more, large changes in the friction of distance will be detected with near certainty in spatial systems comprising 100 or more units. This is a very encouraging finding. We note that there is no obvious tendency for test size to approach its nominal level as n increases, unlike the case of increasing T .

div.head: Intensity of spatial correlation
div.p: To see if the empirical significance levels of the tests are affected by the location of the null hypothesis in (g, r) space, we computed more extensive results for samples of size, T = 25, n = 49. We experimented with (r, g) [ {0.0, +.2, +.4, +.6, +.8} × {1, 2, 3} but found the results were not significantly affected by either the g value, or the sign of r. For all r values, the size of the p5 tests at a nominal level 5% was close to 3%, and the results were not affected by the value of g. Power variations follow the expected pattern, given the results in Tables 2 and 3; that is, as |r| increases, so does test power.

div.head: Functional form, normalization, and scale of disturbances
div.p: To establish how far the qualitative performance of the tests could be affected by functional form, or the normalization of W, the experiments were repeated with the weights based on inverse power of distance, that is, using f {g t , d ij } = d -g ij and with eigenvalue-based normalization, for comparison with those above that use the exponential function and row normalization. The results were very similar, 3 and so are not reported further. To check for sensitivity to the scale of the disturbances relative to the regressors, the innovation variance was set at 0.025, 0.25, or 4.0; we detected no effects on any aspect of test performance, though we are not aware of any formal invariance result.

div.head: SLM
div.p: Similarly, the experiments were repeated for the SLM; the results were in every sense similar, though both empirical significance levels and power were slightly higher, especially for small r for the SLM; with r = 0 and T ≥ 100 the test becomes rather liberal, with empirical significance level in the region of 8% when a 5% nominal level is used. When r , 0 powers are somewhat lower than for positive r, but still impressive. That is, the broad conclusion suggested is that changes in W are more easily detected in the SLM than in the SEM. In the broadest terms, we can conclude for both the SEM and SLM that a change to W induced by a change in the distance-friction parameter, g, at some unknown point in time, can be detected using the test defined at (16) implemented using the critical values tabulated by Andrews (2003), and the risk of falsely detecting such a change is acceptably small. If there is no spatial dependence, here characterized by the case, r = 0, the test becomes somewhat liberal as the time span increases for the SLM, a fact which should be considered in light of the parameter estimates obtained.

div.head: EMPIRICAL ILLUSTRATION: EXCHANGE RATE PASS THROUGH IN THE EURO AREA
div.p: Exchange rate pass-through (ERPT) is a measure of how responsive are international prices to changes in the exchange rate. It is defined as the rate at which changes in exchange rates are reflected in import prices, expressed in the currency of the importing country. In other words, ERPT is the percentage change of import prices in local currency, resulting from a one percent change in the exchange rate between the exporting and importing countries. Recently, passthrough issues have been at the core of the debate over optimal monetary policies.

In the case of euro monetary union, ERPT can be analysed through the prices of imports made by euro area countries from outside the area. Campa and González-Mínguez (2006) and Campa, Goldberg, and González-Mínguez (2005) analyse data for the 12 euro-area members at a sectoral level with a time span of 1989: 1-2001:3. They estimate the industry-specific ERPT across and within countries from data on import prices of 13 different products using a finite distributed lag model for the first-differenced variables:
div.formula: D ln MP t = b 1 + 4 l =0 b 2,l D ln FP t-1 + 4 l=0 b 3,l D ln ER t-1 + U t (17
div.p: where ln MP t is the logarithm of import prices in each country; ln FP t is the logarithm of foreign prices, measured as a world price in US$; and ln ER t is the logarithm of exchange rate against the US$. The short-run ERPT is measured by the coefficient b 3,0 , and the long-run ERPT by the sum 4 l=0 b 3,l . A zero pass-through is consistent with the supposition that exporters fully absorb the fluctuations in exchange rates in their own mark-ups. On the contrary, a unit pass-through is consistent with importers fully absorbing these fluctuations. Campa and González-Mínguez (2006) conclude that in the short-run, ERPT differs across industries and countries and is lower than unity, while in the long-run there is evidence in favour of a full pass-through and the equality of ERPT across industries and countries.

The same case is studied in Banerjee and Carrion-i-Silvestre (2015) to introduce a new cointegration test in the presence of structural breaks and cross-sectional dependence. Using sectoral data for seven countries in the euro area, for the period 1995:1-2005:3, they detect break points dated around the introduction of the euro in January 1999, and around 2002 to reflect entry into the common currency area and the anticipated turbulence in the euro-dollar relation.

We are going to use the same case. To simplify, our approach consists of industry panels, with country cross-sections, for the case of crude materials, inedible, except fuels. We have information (drawn from COMEXT, EUROSTAT) from 1996:1 to 2004:12 for 10 countries: Austria, Au; Finland, Fi; France, Fr; Germany, Ge; Greece, Gr; Ireland, Ir; Italy, It; Netherlands, Ne; Portugal, Po; and Spain, Sp. The main variables appear in Figures 123.

In contrast to Campa and González-Mínguez (2006), we address the ERPT discussion using the so-called autoregressive distributed lag model (ARDL), proposed by Pesaran, Shin, and Smith (2001), which allows us to estimate the long-run relations in the model, 4 irrespective of whether the regressors are I(1) or I(0). Moreover, as in Banerjee and Carrion-i-Silvestre (2015), our specification will also include cross-sectional dependence in the residuals.
Let us define a general SEM-ARDL (p, q1, q2) model as follows:
div.formula: D ln MP t = b 1 + p l=1 b 2,l D ln MP t-l + q 1 l =0 b 3,l D ln FP t-l + q 2 l =0 b 4,l D ln ER t-l +p 1 ln MP t-l + p 2 ln FP t-l + p 3 ln ER t-l + U t U t = rWU t + 1 t ; (t = 1996 : 1 -2004 : 12) ⎫ ⎪ ⎪ ⎬ ⎪ ⎪ ⎭ (18
div.p: We define the W matrix as in expression (4) using an exponential function, f {.}, where d ij is the great-circle distance between the capitals of countries i and j. The matrix has been row-normalized. A higher value of g means a faster decay in the respective distance-decay function. Usual values for g are between 1 and 2 (Ertur & Koch, 2007, set a value of 2 while a value of 1 is very common in the geographically weighted regressions literature; Brunsdom, Fotheringham, & Charlton, 1999). Given this distance decay, and the normalization adopted, the interaction (positive/negative, stronger/weaker) depends on r. Note that the dimensions of this application, (T , n) = (108, 10), are similar to those used in the previous Monte Carlo. Given that there is a strong prior to locate the (possible) break point in 1999/2000, the searching interval is approximately p 5 (2000:1-2000:12).
After the results of Banerjee and Carrion-i-Silvestre (2015), we expect a rejection of model ( 18), which should include structural breaks in some of the regression parameters (including r and g).

We start by determining the appropriate lag lengths p, q1 and q2. Model (18) has been successively estimated for p = q1 = q2 = 1, 2, 3, . . . , 7, paying attention to the assumption of no residual serial correlation (using the Lagrange multiplier tests -LM) and to the Akaike information criterion (AIC). Overall, the results indicate that the minimum lag length to avoid serial correlation is p = q1 = q2 = 4. The null hypothesis of 'no co-integration' is rejected according to the bounds testing procedure of Pesaran et al. (2001). The corresponding F -test takes a value of 8.08, while asymptotic critical value bounds, at a 5% level of significance, are (2.8, 4.01). Furthermore, where possible it is advisable to use parsimonious specifications. Consequently, following Shin and Pesaran (1999), we estimate the 125 models that result from the combinations from 0 to 4 lags of the three variables, looking for the best model (with, simultaneously, co-integration, no residual correlation and best AIC). The equation selected is the SEM -ARDL(1, 4, 0) with main results shown in Table 4.

Table 4 reflects a sequence of estimation and testing steps, as follows. First, when applied to the equation with no breaks, model A in the left-hand panel, the LR (k + 3) d.f. test detects a break in 2000:4. To further explore we estimate model B in the centre panel, which used dummy variables to allow the b parameters to change in 2000:4 but holds the spatial parameters, r and g, constant; testing this constancy assumption in model B the LR 2 d.f. test (see the Appendix in the supplemental data online) detects a break in at least one of the two spatial parameters, in 2000:2, a bit earlier than the break in b incorporated into the model. Accordingly, the next step is to allow for such a change in both cross-sectional coefficients (the LR 1 d.f., directed at testing for changes only in g, proved to be not statistically significant suggesting that the main responsibility for this break is a change in the intensity of cross-sectional dependence, r). Finally we estimate model C, in the right-hand panel, where the breaks in b and in the spatial parameters occur in different months (February and April).

The SEM -ARDL(1, 4, 0) model, under the assumption that there are no break points, model A, gives similar results to the existing literature. The estimated elasticities, either shortor long-run, are positive and lower than 1. Regarding the ERPT mechanism, this means that a 1% change in the exchange rate is not totally transmitted to the price of the importer country, but partially (exactly, 0.82%, in the short-run and 0.84% in the long-run). There is also clear evidence of a positive cross-sectional dependence. More important for us, the LR test with k + 3 d.f. detects a breakpoint in 2000:4. Allowing, first, for a change in the b parameters at that date, in the central panel of Table 4 there is only a slight change in the evidence relating to the ERPT hypothesis. Moreover, the symptoms of cross-sectional dependence are still there and the LR test with 2 d.f. detects an additional breakpoint, affecting just these two parameters, in 2000:2. The right panel shows the estimates corresponding to a break in 2000:4 affecting b and a break in 2000:2 affecting r and g. The elasticities associated with the ERPT mechanism are higher for the second subsample, and the structure of cross-sectional dependence has changed: only for the first period, prior to 2000:2, do both parameters remain statistically significant. Given that the estimation of r in the second period is not statistically different from zero, we omit the estimate of g because this parameter, in this situation, is not identified. A natural interpretation of this result is that, as detected by the 2 d.f. test, the intensity of the spatial dependence, measured by r, has fallen dramatically after the break, resulting in both a lack of power in the 1 d.f. test and a lack of precision in the post-break estimate of g.

We might say that the introduction of the euro has favoured the creation of a truly, more unified single market where the basic factors shaping pricing imports are, in fact, world prices and the exchange rate (ERPT is tested below). The impact of individual shocks are purely transient and local.

Finally, we test whether the ERPT elasticity is equal to 1, either in the short-or long-run. Results appear in Table 5. The null hypothesis is rejected in the short-run for the case of no breaks (model A). The introduction, as detected, of a partial break in 2000:4, in model B, combined with a break in the cross-sectional coefficients in 2000:2, model C, leads to the rejection of the null but only in the first period. Regarding the long-run, all three models show evidence of complete passthrough (unitary elasticity is not rejected).

Hence, the conclusion that we draw from this exercise is clear: if the structural breaks are not properly treated, short-run conclusions (in the case of ERPT) can be severely misleading. This problem can be avoided by allowing for parametric changes, guided by appropriate use of the structural change tests introduced in this paper.

div.head: DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS
div.p: If the functional form for the weight matrix can be assumed, up to an unknown distance friction parameter, g, then this parameter may be estimated by ML from a single-data cross-section. If a panel of such cross sections is available, it is possible to detect a change in g, when a change has occurred, even at an unknown change point. Test power increases as the space or time (n, T ) dimension of the data increases, and tests using asymptotic critical values become less conservative, judged against nominal significance levels, as T increases. Powers are higher when the spatial interaction is relatively intense, represented in the Monte Carlo experiments here by null 2 and alternative 2, and in general slightly higher for the SLM than for the SEM.

In the experiments we considered weights that were functions of Euclidean distance between the nodes of a square lattice, being of either exponential or inverse power form. The same approach could be adopted for a wide class of possible functional forms, and indeed more general weight functions unrelated to 'distance', as well as to more elaborate models than the SEM or SLM studied here. We did not experiment with changes in the regression coefficients, b, because we wished to focus attention here on testing the weight matrix; however, this possibility is easily accommodated into the tests and was implemented in the empirical exercise reported above. The tests did indeed detect breaks in parameters, with plausible dates, in our real sample of T = 108 observations for n = 10 countries. Exploring the possibility of breaks in the weight function over time is likely to prove worthwhile in a variety of other empirical settings.
